Meteg after the primary stress

A meteg almost always comes before the stressed syllable of its word, but it can also come after the stress. MAM has 232 cases of meteg after the stress (MAS).

For example:

Gen. 22:7 — הִנֶּ֣נִּֽי בְנִ֑י

In this document, by "word" we mean either a simple word (having just one atom) or a compound word (having two or more atoms connected by maqaf marks). By "atom", we mean a sequence of pointed letters uninterrupted by space, maqaf, or any other punctuation.

The location of a word's stress is not always obvious. In this document, we locate stress using Phonetic MAM, an edition of MAM that marks the stress of every word in MAM.

MAS census by cantillation system

cant-sys words MBS MAS % MAS
prose 233,586 13,091 178 1.3%
poetic 29,605 1,814 54 2.9%
all 263,191 14,905 232 1.5%

So a meteg comes before the stress 14,905 times and after it 232 times.

The prose row in the table above is for the 21 books plus the verses of Job's prose frame; the poetic row is for the verses of Job's main, poetic section plus all Psalms and the whole book of Proverbs. Only one cantillation (φ1) of dually cantillated passages participates in every analysis on this page, including the census above.

General facts about MAS

  • In every MAS case, the MAS immediately follows the stress syllable.
  • In every MAS case, the stress syllable has a conjunctive accent (φ2).
  • In every MAS case but one, the next word has initial stress (φ3).
  • In every MAS case except four (φ4), the MAS syllable is final.

The three types of MAS

All but 7 cases of MAS can be sorted into one of the three following types: φ5

  • In type 1, the MAS is on an open final syllable.
  • In type 2, the word is closed by a guttural.
  • In type 3, the MAS is on a closed, final, tsere-vowelled syllable. (φ6)
Type Prose Poetic All Example
1 113 10 123 הִנֶּ֣נִּֽי בְנִ֑י
2 34 26 60 תַּצְמִ֣יחַֽ לָ֑ךְ
3 26 16 42 וַיָּ֣צֵֽץ צִ֔יץ
misc 5 2 7 וַיֹּ֥אמֶֽר ׀ לֹ֖א

It is natural to ask how often a MAS actually appears in situations fit for a MAS, i.e. in situations conforming to the criteria of one of the three MAS types. The answer is that a MAS actually appears only 0.8% of the time in situations fit for MAS. (φ7)

The meteg sharing a letter with oleh

6 meteg marks share a letter with oleh. The table labels each meteg as MBS or MAS.

Ps. 2:7 אֶֽ֫ל־חֹ֥ק MBS
Ps. 78:38 וְֽלֹא־יַֽ֫שְׁחִ֥ית MBS
Ps. 80:15 שֽׁ֫וּב־נָ֥א MBS
Job 14:14 הֲיִֽ֫חְיֶ֥ה MBS
Ps. 37:7 וְהִתְח֢וֹלֵֽ֫ל ל֥וֹ MAS
Prov. 8:34 שֹׁמֵ֢עַֽ֫ לִ֥י MAS

We count each such meteg as if the oleh were not there, because oleh is not an accent indicating stress, even when it is the last accent in the word, as it is in the MAS rows above. In other words, a MAS word with a meteg might at first look like some weird "meteg on the stress" (neither before nor after), but it is not!

Footnotes

φ1 — Dually cantillated passages

MAM has dual-cantillation templates in the two Decalogues and Genesis 35:22. The analyses presented in this document use only the cant-alef branch of each template. The table below shows that this choice has no effect on the MAS count and changes the other two counts only by 1.

count cant-alef cant-bet
Words 130 129
MBS 12 13
MAS 0 0

Only Deut. 5:14 differs in the number of words. cant-alef has two words where cant-bet has one maqaf compound.

cant-alef כ֣י ע֤בד
cant-bet כי־ע֥בד

Only Deut. 5:6 differs in metegs before the stress. cant-bet has one meteg before the stress in the word below; cant-alef has the two words below, neither with a meteg.

cant-alef לֹא־יִהְיֶ֥ה לְךָ֛ no meteg
cant-bet לֹ֣א יִהְיֶֽה־לְךָ֩ MBS

φ2 — A meteg after silluq in Leningrad

In the Leningrad Codex, the last word of 1 Samuel 17:5 seems to have a meteg after its silluq.

Although that meteg is pretty surprising, we deem it less surprising than if we interpret the marks in meteg-silluq order. In silluq-meteg order, only the presence of the meteg is surprising; in meteg-silluq order, the location of the stress is surprising. We find a meteg surprise far more likely than a stress surprise.

This surprising meteg is correctly recorded in BHS and in BHS-derived editions such as UXLC and WLC:

MAM נְחֹֽשֶׁת׃
BHS נְחֹֽשֶֽׁת׃

A meteg after a silluq is hard to identify in Unicode, since the two marks share one codepoint.

φ3 — Jer. 46:14

At Jer. 46:14, the word after the MAS lacks initial stress: וְהַשְׁמִ֣יעֽוּ בְמִגְדּ֔וֹל.

φ4 — The four nonfinal MAS syllables

The four exceptions are type-2 MAS cases: each MAS syllable is an open penultimate tsere syllable before a final furtive-pataḥ syllable.

Isa. 63:12 בּ֤וֹקֵֽעַ מַ֙יִם֙
Prov. 1:19 כׇּל־בֹּ֣צֵֽעַ בָּ֑צַע
Prov. 11:26 מֹ֣נֵֽעַ בָּ֭ר
Job 5:10 וְשֹׁ֥לֵֽחַ מַ֝֗יִם

φ5 — Sources for types 1–3

The three types of MAS are described in both ITM and CoS. Exactly what words are included and excluded in these three types vary between ITM, CoS, and our document here, but they broadly agree.

Type ITM CoS CoS-pg
1 §332 §3(j), §§46-47 300; 354; 355
2 §354 §3(b), §§9-10 299; 308; 309
3 §338, fed by §308 §3(a), §§5-8 299; 301; 302; 306; 307

φ6 — Do types 2 and 3 overlap?

Types 2 and 3 could in principle overlap. However, 56 of the 60 type-2 MAS syllables have pataḥ, and while the other 4 have tsere, that syllable is not only open but also nonfinal. Thus no type-2 MAS meets the type-3 condition. Indeed, words with a final tsere syllable closed by a guttural are quite rare even without a meteg. Only 154 words have a final tsere syllable closed by a guttural. All 154 occur in Aramaic and end in a mappiq he: 136 are in Daniel and 18 are in Ezra. An example is as follows:

Dan. 2:5 — וּפִשְׁרֵ֔הּ

φ7 — Fit for MAS

"Fit for MAS" is analogous to the broader idea of a syllable fit for a meteg. It means that a syllable has one or more of the three structures below. The table records how often MAM has MAS in each structure and how often MAM lacks MAS there.

Type Fit for MAS Has MAS Lacks MAS
1 23,850 123 23,727
2 4,083 60 4,023
3 43 42 1
any of the three types 27,976 225 27,751
